title: Strategy & Revision
scopeHtml: Scope: choosing a pattern from clues, interview communication, edge cases, language differences for a C++ developer.

notes.title: Pattern cheat sheet: clue to technique
notes.html:
Read the problem for signal words, then jump to the matching pattern. If two patterns fit, start with the cheaper one.

Clue in the problem Pattern Typical cost
"pair/triple with sum", sorted array Two pointers O(n) or O(n²)
"contiguous subarray/substring", "longest/shortest window" Sliding window O(n)
"subarray sum equals K", negatives allowed Prefix sum + hash map O(n)
"seen before", duplicates, counting, anagrams Hash map / set O(n)
sorted input, "find position", "minimise the maximum" Binary search (on index or answer) O(log n)
"next greater/smaller", histogram, nested matching Monotonic stack O(n)
"k-th largest", "top K", "merge sorted", scheduling Heap O(n log k)
overlapping ranges, calendars Sort + sweep (or heap) O(n log n)
tree or "hierarchy" DFS recursion / BFS levels O(n)
prefix lookups, autocomplete Trie O(L)
grid, connected regions DFS/BFS flood fill O(rows × cols)
fewest steps, unweighted BFS O(V + E)
prerequisites, ordering, build Topological sort O(V + E)
"are these connected?", merging groups Union-Find ~O(1)
weighted shortest path Dijkstra (no negatives) O((V+E) log V)
"count ways", "min/max cost", choices with overlap Dynamic programming varies
"all combinations/permutations/subsets", n ≤ 20 Backtracking exponential
parity, pairs cancelling, flags Bit manipulation O(n)
"best local choice is provably safe" Greedy O(n log n)

Industry examples. The same decision table is how senior engineers pick tools at work: a cache is a hash map, a scheduler is a heap, a dependency resolver is a topological sort, and a recommender is a graph or DP.

Everyday analogy. A doctor does not run every test; symptoms point to the likely diagnosis, and a cheap test confirms it.

Common interview traps.

  • Memorising solutions instead of signals; a new twist breaks memorisation.
  • Choosing an advanced structure (segment tree) when a simple one (prefix sum) is enough.
  • Ignoring constraints: n ≤ 20 hints exponential, n ≤ 10^5 hints O(n log n).

notes.title: How to communicate in a coding interview
notes.html:
The interviewer grades how you think as much as the final code. A reliable script:

  1. Clarify (1-2 minutes): input range, duplicates, empty input, negative numbers, sorted or not, memory limits, what to return when impossible.
  2. Examples: walk through a normal case and an edge case.
  3. Brute force: state it and its complexity, even if it is too slow. This shows a baseline and a safe fallback.
  4. Optimise: name the pattern and why it applies ("the array is sorted, so two pointers can discard candidates").
  5. Agree on the plan before typing: "Does that approach sound good?"
  6. Code cleanly with meaningful names, narrating key decisions.
  7. Test by hand: run your own example line by line, then edge cases (empty, one element, duplicates, large values).
  8. Analyse: time and space; mention trade-offs and what you would do with more time.

If you are stuck: restate the problem, try a smaller example, think about what information the brute force repeats, and ask a clarifying question rather than going silent.

Industry examples. Real code review and design discussions use the same loop: clarify requirements, propose, justify, test.

Everyday analogy. A navigator announcing the route before driving so the driver can correct a wrong turn early.

Common interview traps.

  • Silent coding for 20 minutes, giving the interviewer nothing to evaluate.
  • Not testing; a bug that you find yourself is far better than one the interviewer finds.
  • Arguing about a hint instead of using it.

notes.title: Edge cases and testing checklist
notes.html:
Before you say "done", mentally run these:

  • Empty input ([], "", null) and single element.
  • Duplicates and all elements equal.
  • Negative numbers, zero, and the minimum/maximum integer (overflow).
  • Sorted, reverse sorted, and already-solved inputs.
  • Boundaries: first and last index, window size equal to n, k = 0 or k > n.
  • Disconnected graphs, cycles, self-loops, unreachable targets.
  • Large input: will recursion overflow the stack? Is O(n²) too slow?

A fast way to test is to write 3 tiny cases as comments next to the function and trace them.

Industry examples. Property-based testing tools (Hypothesis, QuickCheck) automate exactly this: they generate empty, huge and extreme inputs.

Everyday analogy. Proofreading a document by checking the first line, the last line and the strangest paragraph.

Common interview traps.

  • Off-by-one at the boundaries.
  • Integer overflow on sums and products (use long).
  • Mutating the input when the problem implies it must stay unchanged.

notes.title: C++ to Java, Kotlin and Python quick reference
notes.html:
You know C++; this table maps the everyday tools you need in interviews.

Need C++ Java Kotlin Python
Dynamic array vector<int> ArrayList<Integer> MutableList<Int> / ArrayList list
Hash map unordered_map HashMap HashMap / mutableMapOf dict
Hash set unordered_set HashSet HashSet / mutableSetOf set
Ordered map map TreeMap sortedMapOf / TreeMap sortedcontainers or bisect
Stack stack / vector ArrayDeque ArrayDeque list
Queue / deque queue, deque ArrayDeque ArrayDeque collections.deque
Heap (min) priority_queue with greater PriorityQueue (min by default) PriorityQueue heapq
Sort sort(v.begin(), v.end()) Arrays.sort, Collections.sort sorted(), sort() sorted(), .sort()
Big ints long long long Long built in
String builder string += StringBuilder StringBuilder "".join(list)
Min / max min, max Math.min minOf, maxOf min, max

Custom sorting differs the most. Sort pairs by the second value, descending:

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
vector<pair<int,int>> v = {{1, 5}, {2, 9}, {3, 2}};
sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](auto& a, auto& b) { return a.second > b.second; });
int[][] v = {{1, 5}, {2, 9}, {3, 2}};
Arrays.sort(v, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(b[1], a[1]));      // avoid a[1] - b[1]: overflow risk
val v = listOf(1 to 5, 2 to 9, 3 to 2)
val sorted = v.sortedByDescending { it.second }
v = [(1, 5), (2, 9), (3, 2)]
v.sort(key=lambda p: p[1], reverse=True)

Differences that cause bugs for a C++ developer.

  • Integer overflow: C++ signed overflow is undefined; Java and Kotlin wrap silently; Python never overflows.
  • Integer division truncates toward zero in all of C++, Java and Kotlin; Python's // floors (-7 // 2 == -4).
  • References and copying: Java/Kotlin/Python store references to objects; list2 = list1 does not copy in Python, and adding a list to a result requires cur[:] or new ArrayList<>(cur).
  • Strings are immutable in Java, Kotlin and Python; build with StringBuilder or "".join(...) inside loops to avoid O(n²).
  • Recursion limit: Python defaults to about 1,000 frames; Java's default stack handles roughly 10,000 deep; C++ depends on the stack size.
  • Null safety: Kotlin separates T and T?; Java and Python use null/None freely.
  • Speed: Python is roughly 10-50× slower than C++ for tight loops; interview time limits assume reasonable constants, but know when to prefer Java or C++.

Industry examples. Backend services at many companies are Java or Kotlin; data and scripting work uses Python; performance-critical systems use C++.

Everyday analogy. Driving a car abroad: the pedals are the same but the side of the road differs, and that is where mistakes happen.

Common interview traps.

  • a[1] - b[1] as a comparator in Java overflows for large values; use Integer.compare.
  • Assuming Python's // and C++'s / behave the same for negatives.
  • Using Python for a problem at the limit of its speed without checking constraints.

notes.title: Four-week revision plan
notes.html:
A realistic plan for about 1-1.5 hours a day. For each topic, read the notes section, solve the questions, then re-implement from memory in your two most-used languages. Spaced repetition on the web app helps.

Week Focus Goal
1 Arrays and hashing, two pointers and windows, binary search and greedy Solve 15-20 problems; recognise signals instantly
2 Lists, stacks and queues, heaps and intervals, trees and tries Write each template from memory in C++ and one other language
3 Graphs (BFS, DFS, topological sort, union-find, Dijkstra), start DP Handle grids and dependency graphs confidently
4 Dynamic programming, backtracking and bits, mixed review and mock interviews Timed 45-minute sessions, explain aloud, test edge cases

Weekly rhythm. Days 1-4: learn and solve new problems. Day 5: redo problems you failed or needed hints for. Day 6: timed mock interview. Day 7: rest or light review.

Tracking. Keep a one-line "mistake log" (what pattern you missed, what bug bit you). Review it before every mock.

Industry examples. Engineers who interview well usually practise a modest number of problems repeatedly with deliberate review, not hundreds once.

Everyday analogy. Learning a language: short daily practice with review beats cramming.

Common interview traps.

  • Grinding hundreds of problems without reviewing mistakes.
  • Skipping mock interviews, then freezing when explaining aloud.
  • Learning all four languages at once; pick one primary language for interviews, and use the others for breadth.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html: Map clues to patterns (sorted pairs: two pointers; contiguous window: sliding window; sum with negatives: prefix sums; shortest steps: BFS; dependencies: topological sort; weighted routes: Dijkstra; overlapping choices: DP; all arrangements: backtracking). In the interview clarify, give a brute force first, name the pattern, plan, code, test edge cases by hand, then analyse complexity. Watch the language differences that bite a C++ developer: overflow, integer division on negatives, reference copying and immutable strings. Follow a four-week plan of learn, solve, redo, mock, and keep a mistake log.

questions.promptHtml: A problem says "find the longest subarray with at most K distinct values" and n = 10^5. How do you decide which technique to use?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you map signals and constraints to a technique, rather than guessing.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Contiguous subarray" plus "longest" with a condition that gets worse as the window grows points to a variable sliding window. With n = 10^5 I need O(n) or O(n log n), and a window with a count map gives O(n): expand the right end, and shrink the left end while there are more than K distinct values.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The checklist: Is it contiguous? Is the condition monotonic in the window (adding elements can only break it)? Are values non-negative if the condition is a sum? Here distinct count is monotonic, so a window works. If the condition were a sum with negatives, I would use prefix sums with a hash map instead.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int longestKDistinct(vector<int>& a, int k) {
    unordered_map<int, int> cnt;
    int l = 0, best = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < (int)a.size(); r++) {
        cnt[a[r]]++;
        while ((int)cnt.size() > k) {                  // too many distinct: shrink
            if (--cnt[a[l]] == 0) cnt.erase(a[l]);
            l++;
        }
        best = max(best, r - l + 1);
    }
    return best;
}
int longestKDistinct(int[] a, int k) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> cnt = new HashMap<>();
    int l = 0, best = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < a.length; r++) {
        cnt.merge(a[r], 1, Integer::sum);
        while (cnt.size() > k) {                       // too many distinct: shrink
            if (cnt.merge(a[l], -1, Integer::sum) == 0) cnt.remove(a[l]);
            l++;
        }
        best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1);
    }
    return best;
}
fun longestKDistinct(a: IntArray, k: Int): Int {
    val cnt = HashMap<Int, Int>()
    var l = 0
    var best = 0
    for (r in a.indices) {
        cnt[a[r]] = (cnt[a[r]] ?: 0) + 1
        while (cnt.size > k) {                         // too many distinct: shrink
            val c = cnt[a[l]]!! - 1
            if (c == 0) cnt.remove(a[l]) else cnt[a[l]] = c
            l++
        }
        best = maxOf(best, r - l + 1)
    }
    return best
}
from collections import defaultdict

def longest_k_distinct(a, k):
    cnt = defaultdict(int)
    l = best = 0
    for r, x in enumerate(a):
        cnt[x] += 1
        while len(cnt) > k:                            # too many distinct: shrink
            cnt[a[l]] -= 1
            if cnt[a[l]] == 0:
                del cnt[a[l]]
            l += 1
        best = max(best, r - l + 1)
    return best

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting to remove a key when its count reaches zero, so size() overstates the distinct count.
  • Using a window when the condition is not monotonic.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Exactly K distinct? → atMost(K) - atMost(K - 1).
  2. Sum condition with negatives? → Prefix sums with a hash map.
  3. Complexity? → O(n) time, O(K) space.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior states the monotonicity test and the "exactly K" trick.

questions.promptHtml: You are given an unfamiliar problem and have no idea how to start. What do you do in the first five minutes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: They watch how you handle uncertainty, which is the daily reality of engineering.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I clarify inputs, constraints and edge cases, write two examples including an edge case, and state the brute-force solution with its complexity. That gives me a baseline and often reveals the repeated work I can eliminate with a pattern. I share my thinking aloud and agree on a plan before coding.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: If still stuck, simplify: solve a smaller or special case (sorted input, n = 3), look at what the brute force recomputes, and ask what data structure would make that lookup O(1). Asking a targeted question is fine and is often how real engineers work; going silent is the worst option.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Jumping to code without examples or constraints.
  • Presenting only a final optimal answer with no baseline.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. You find a bug while coding? → Say so, trace an example, fix it calmly.
  2. The interviewer gives a hint? → Acknowledge it and build on it.
  3. You run out of time? → Explain the remaining steps and complexity of your approach.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior structures the conversation (clarify, brute force, optimise, test) and manages time.

questions.promptHtml: Which edge cases do you check for a function that takes an array and returns a number, before you say it is done?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Bugs usually hide at the boundaries.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Empty array, single element, all duplicates, negatives and zero, maximum and minimum integers (overflow), already sorted and reverse sorted, and the boundary indices. I trace two or three of these through the code by hand and mention complexity.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: For graphs add disconnected components, cycles, self-loops and unreachable targets; for windows add k = 0, k > n and k = n. Use 64-bit integers for sums and products. Decide what to return for invalid input (throw, -1, empty).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Off-by-one errors at index boundaries.
  • Overflow on sums and products.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you test it in a real codebase? → Unit tests plus property-based tests generating extreme inputs.
  2. Should you validate input? → Clarify: assume valid in an interview, validate at trust boundaries in production.
  3. How do you find an off-by-one quickly? → Trace a size-1 and size-2 example.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior mentions property-based testing and defensive behaviour at API boundaries.

questions.promptHtml: You usually write C++ but must use Java or Python in an interview. Which differences are most likely to cause bugs?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Practical language fluency matters in polyglot teams.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Integer behaviour (Java and Kotlin wrap on overflow, Python never overflows), integer division on negatives (Python's // floors while C++, Java and Kotlin truncate toward zero), reference semantics (assigning a list does not copy it, so copy before storing results), immutable strings (use StringBuilder or join in loops), the recursion limit in Python, and comparator syntax, where a - b can overflow in Java.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Examples: -7 / 2 is -3 in C++/Java/Kotlin but -7 // 2 is -4 in Python. In Java use Integer.compare(a, b) for comparators. In Python add sys.setrecursionlimit or write the iterative version for deep recursion. Pick one primary interview language and know its standard library well (collections, sorting with a key, heaps).

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
vector<pair<int,int>> v = {{1, 5}, {2, 9}, {3, 2}};
sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](auto& a, auto& b) { return a.second > b.second; });
int[][] v = {{1, 5}, {2, 9}, {3, 2}};
Arrays.sort(v, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(b[1], a[1]));
val v = listOf(1 to 5, 2 to 9, 3 to 2)
val sorted = v.sortedByDescending { it.second }
v = [(1, 5), (2, 9), (3, 2)]
v.sort(key=lambda p: p[1], reverse=True)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• a[1] - b[1] as a Java comparator overflowing.
  • Assuming Python and C++ round division the same way for negatives.
  • Storing a reference to a mutable list instead of a copy.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is Python slower and when does it matter? → Interpreted loops are 10-50× slower; fine for logic, risky at the constraint limit.
  2. Kotlin null safety? → T? types force handling of absence at compile time.
  3. Which language would you pick for an interview? → The one you are fastest and safest in, usually with strong collections.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior lists specific traps and chooses a language deliberately.

questions.contextHtml: You have four weeks before a product-company interview. You know basic arrays and recursion but have not practised data structures in two years. You have about 90 minutes on weekdays and 3 hours on one weekend day. Last time you solved 80 random problems and still froze on a graph question.
questions.promptHtml: How would you structure the four weeks?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Solve as many problems as possible" with no structure or review.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which companies and levels? Which languages are allowed? Which topics were weakest last time?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Start with a diagnostic: a few problems per pattern to find weak areas.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Random practice leaves gaps in patterns; no review means mistakes repeat; no timed or spoken practice causes freezing.
  4. How I'd verify: Track solved-without-hints rate per pattern and time to solve.
  5. Root cause: Unstructured, unreviewed practice rather than too few problems.
  6. Fix: Weeks 1-2: core patterns (hashing, two pointers and windows, binary search, stacks and heaps, trees) with the notes first, then 3-4 problems per pattern, and rewriting each template from memory. Week 3: graphs and the start of DP. Week 4: DP, backtracking, mixed sets and two timed mock interviews with explaining aloud. Redo failed problems after 2 and 7 days. Keep a mistake log.
  7. Prevention: A weekly review slot and a rule to explain solutions aloud.
  8. Trade-offs: Depth over breadth means fewer total problems but stronger recognition; some rare topics (segment trees, advanced graph algorithms) are deliberately skipped.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• You are failing graph problems? → Add more BFS/DFS on grids first, then topological sort and union-find.
  • Only 2 weeks left? → Focus on the top patterns (hash maps, two pointers, windows, binary search, trees, BFS/DFS, basic DP) and mock interviews.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A candidate who solved 60 problems with deliberate review and weekly mocks outperformed peers who had solved 300 without review.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: random grinding.
  • Hire: a pattern-based plan with review.
  • Strong hire: diagnostics, spaced repetition, mock interviews, mistake log and prioritisation by time left.
